strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the visual-token cost of multimodal language models. Combining attention-based outlier selection with key-similarity merging provides a simple, modular approach, and the figures clearly explain the pipeline.

PruMerge+ demonstrates a promising accuracy–compression trade-off. With 25% of visual tokens and LoRA fine-tuning, the 7B model achieves 76.8 versus 78.5 on VQAv2 and 64.9 versus 64.3 on MMBench (Table 1). Substantial token reduction with these accuracy differences is potentially useful.

Evaluation covers six image benchmarks, two language-model sizes, and three video benchmarks. Training-free integration into Video-LLaVA is particularly encouraging: Table 3 largely preserves performance and improves ActivityNet-QA accuracy from 45.3 to 48.3 with PruMerge.

The ablations provide useful evidence against simple sampling alternatives. At 40 tokens, training-free PruMerge achieves 54.0 on TextVQA versus 47.42 for the better spatial-sampling baseline (Table 4). The paper also examines fine-tuning effects and attributes its underlying models, datasets, and methodological building blocks.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not sufficiently establish the proposed method's advantage over existing token-reduction approaches. Table 4 compares only sequential and uniform spatial sampling. Budget-matched attention top-k selection, the cited token-merging approach, and pooling would be stronger controls. Accuracy–cost curves and matched fine-tuning budgets are needed to establish the specific contribution of adaptive IQR selection and merging.

Practical acceleration remains unverified. Table 2 reports roofline-model estimates for LLM prefill under one image/prompt configuration, without measured end-to-end latency, throughput, or peak memory. These estimates do not establish the effects of selection/clustering overhead, visual encoding, variable-length batching, and decoding. PruMerge+, which provides the strongest accuracy trade-off, lacks a corresponding efficiency evaluation.

The aggressive-compression results do not support repeated claims of preserving performance without compromise. For the 7B model, VQAv2 falls from 78.5 to 72.0, POPE from 85.9 to 76.3, and MME from 1510.7 to 1350.3 (Table 1). These losses may be acceptable for some efficiency-sensitive applications, but they materially qualify the claimed preservation of visual reasoning.

Important implementation details are ambiguous or missing. Algorithm 1 adds m uniformly sampled tokens to m selected tokens, which does not explain PruMerge+'s reported 25% retention given PruMerge's 5.5%. The neighbor count k is unspecified, and the update uses an unnormalized neighbor sum while the text also describes weighted averaging. Attention-head aggregation and LoRA training hyperparameters are insufficiently documented. These issues hinder reproduction of the reported trade-off.
